native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among Black respondents in this NLSY-processed sample (n=2,465 after dedup; 124 ever jailed 1985–1994), ever being jailed is associated with substantially lower wealth in 1996 across every initial-wealth stratum, and the wealth penalty is non-uniform — amplified at the bottom of the wealth distribution and attenuated at the top: jailed Black respondents in the lowest and middle 1985-wealth tertiles collapse to a median 1996 wealth of $0 (≈100% penalty relative to non-jailed peers), those in the highest tertile retain about a quarter (−74%), and the shortfall in 1985→1996 wealth accumulation (mean asinh-transformed growth) attenuates monotonically from −5.60 asinh units in the lowest tertile to −3.33 in the middle and −2.57 in the highest.
native_result.WorkflowB: Stage 1 — Clean: load nls_incarceration_processed.csv, normalize 'hipanic'→'hispanic', drop 1,899 full-row duplicates (12,013 → 10,114 rows). Stage 2 — Stratify: within Black subsample, compute tertile cut-points of composite_wealth_1985 (USD 20, 5,508); documented downgrade from quintiles because Q2 × ever_jailed=1 had n=7 (<30 threshold); all tertile cells ≥38. Stage 3 — Headline: report medians of W1985/W1990/W1996, median W1996 penalty (j1−j0), and mean asinh growth 1985→1996 penalty by tertile × ever_jailed. Stage 4 — Secondary: sex-disaggregated medians (reported only as secondary per guardrail, since female-T3 cell is small) and cross-race context (own-race tertile breakpoints). All outputs associative/descriptive; no causal language.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black respondents, ever being jailed in 1985–1994 is associated with substantially lower median 1996 wealth in every 1985-wealth tertile, with a larger proportional penalty at the bottom than at the top.
sub_hypo.context: Black respondents in the processed NLSY 1979 cohort after full-row deduplication (n=2,465; 124 ever jailed in 1985–1994), stratified by within-Black 1985-wealth tertiles with cut-points of $20 and $5,508; all tertile-by-incarceration cells have at least 38 respondents.
sub_hypo.relations: Within each initial-wealth tertile, ever-jailed respondents have lower median 1996 wealth than non-jailed peers. Ever-jailed respondents in the lowest and middle tertiles have median 1996 wealth of $0 (approximately 100% penalties), whereas those in the highest tertile retain about a quarter of non-jailed peers' median wealth (74% penalty). This non-uniform association is descriptive, not causal.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black respondents, the shortfall in mean asinh-transformed wealth growth from 1985 to 1996 associated with ever being jailed attenuates monotonically as initial-wealth tertile increases.
sub_hypo.context: Black respondents in the processed NLSY 1979 cohort after full-row deduplication (n=2,465; 124 ever jailed in 1985–1994), stratified by within-Black 1985-wealth tertiles with cut-points of $20 and $5,508; all tertile-by-incarceration cells have at least 38 respondents.
sub_hypo.relations: The ever-jailed minus non-jailed difference in mean asinh-transformed 1985–1996 wealth growth is −5.60 asinh units in the lowest initial-wealth tertile, −3.33 in the middle, and −2.57 in the highest. The negative association weakens monotonically with increasing initial wealth; it is descriptive, not causal.
